meta.title: Mandarin Chinese — Bopomofo
meta.subtitle: 62 zhuyin symbols, tone marks and combinations — beside Pinyin and tones
meta.desc: Bopomofo (zhuyin), the phonetic script taught in Taiwan and printed on every vocabulary card on this shelf beside the pinyin: 62 notes, one card each — the five tone marks, the 37 symbols (21 consonants, 13 vowels and the three medials ㄧ ㄨ ㄩ) and the 20 two-symbol combinations, several of which pinyin spells in a way the symbols do not suggest (ㄧㄡ is -iu, ㄨㄥ is -ong, ㄩㄥ is -iong). The front shows the symbol; the back gives its pinyin, its sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet, how the sound is made, the character the shape comes from, and up to three words from the Level 1 to 3 decks written in bopomofo, with a speaker beside each and the symbol picked out. THE ORDER is the article's: tones, consonants (ㄅ ㄆ ㄇ ㄈ …), vowels, medials, combinations. Pinyin and tones is the deck to start with; this one is for a learner who reads Taiwanese materials or types with a zhuyin keyboard. At the default of ten new cards a day it takes 7 days. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: ㄪ, ㄫ, ㄬ and ㄭ, which the article says are no longer used for Mandarin, and handwriting or stroke order. No description is written for this deck: each is quoted, with a cut marked […]; a symbol with no exact pinyin counterpart (ㄛ, ㄝ) has no sound description, and a seal-script picture in an origin is left out. — Symbols, origins, IPA, pinyin equivalents and tone notes: Wikipedia, “Bopomofo”, revision 1385906035 of 2026-11-15. How each sound is made: Wikipedia, “Pinyin”, revision 1384755350 of 2026-11-09 (both CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, bopomofo, readings and meanings: the HSK 3.0 Level 1 to 3 decks on this shelf (the official HSK 3.0 vocabulary lists, and CC-CEDICT, CC BY-SA 4.0).

bopomofo.name: Mandarin bopomofo

fields.Says: First tone is a high-level tone. It is a steady high sound, produced as if it were being sung instead of spoken.
fields.Note: In bopomofo, the mark for first tone is usually omitted but can be included […].
fields.Examples:
as in
他ㄊㄚtāhe
一ㄧyīone
三ㄙㄢsānthree

fields.Says: Second tone is a rising tone. It is usually described as a high-rising (35), with the sound that rises from middle to high pitch (like in the English "What?!").
fields.Note: […] tone marks for the second, third, and fourth tones are shared between bopomofo and pinyin.
fields.Examples:
as in
您ㄋㄧㄣˊnínyou [polite form]
十ㄕˊshíten
零ㄌㄧㄥˊlíngzero

fields.Says: Third tone is a low tone. It is also often termed a "dipping tone". This tone is often demonstrated as having a rise in pitch after the low fall; […] When a third-tone syllable is not said in isolation, this rise is normally heard only if it appears at the end of a sentence or before a pause, and then usually only on stressed monosyllables.
fields.Note: […] tone marks for the second, third, and fourth tones are shared between bopomofo and pinyin.
fields.Examples:
as in
请ㄑㄧㄥˇqǐngto invite
我ㄨㄛˇwǒI
你ㄋㄧˇnǐyou

fields.Says: Fourth tone is a falling tone. It features a sharp fall from high to lower pitch (as is heard in curt commands in English, such as "Stop!").
fields.Note: […] tone marks for the second, third, and fourth tones are shared between bopomofo and pinyin.
fields.Examples:
as in
是ㄕˋshìto be
不ㄅㄨˋbùnot
二ㄦˋèrtwo

fields.Says: Also called fifth tone or zeroth tone […], the neutral tone is sometimes thought of as a lack of tone. It is associated with weak syllables, which are generally somewhat shorter than tonic syllables. […] The pitch of a syllable with neutral tone is determined by the tone of the preceding syllable.
fields.Note: […] a dot above indicates the fifth tone (also known as the neutral tone). The vocabulary decks on this shelf print the dot after the syllable (ㄗ˙); the article’s own example writes it before (˙ㄗ).
